segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Hey everybody, Peter Zahn here coming to you from the Chicago Lakeshore.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Today's topic is China's difficulty in securing energy supplies from really about anywhere.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The trigger for me for this one is something that happened a couple weeks ago.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We had one of the regional chiefs of a group called TTP, the name is right here,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: also known as the Pakistani Taliban.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Now, for those of you who have not blocked out the entire 20 years of the war on terror,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: you'll remember the TTP was one of the groups that really plagued the United States

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: in getting supplies from the Guar port in western Pakistan up into Afghanistan.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: A secondary route was going for Karachi North.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: TTP controls a lot of the countryside.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: A lot of western and especially northern Pakistan is dry to desert and rugged and mountainous.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And so you can easily have a militant group that just snarls supply lines.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Anyway, this guy, a couple weeks ago, said that he's perfectly willing to allow the Chinese

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: to build their massive infrastructure project through Pakistan as long as his tribe gets 5% protection money.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Which, you know, is kind of novel that he's got a business model like that.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Anyway, he means it and he's made it very clear that he and his people are willing to attack

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: the infrastructure, the construction sites, and the workers.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: He made that very explicit in his statements.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And it kind of leaves the Chinese reeling.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: One of the things that people forget about the Chinese is there's always this weird assumption

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: in the West and China is that China is somehow different from all of the powers that have come before.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And if you just introduce a new major power to the area,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: everyone's going to just buddy up to them because they're not what came before.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And that's just never true.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The Chinese generate just as much mal-feeling as everybody else.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And they're seen as just another imperial power in most zones.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And for the Chinese, this has always been more of a problem than has been for the Western powers.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Because if you're Britain or France or Spain or any of the old imperial set,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: yes, there's always issues with getting access to energy.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: But you're relatively proximate to a lot of them.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So, for example, if you're, say, just France, you know, Algeria is right across the Mediterranean as is Libya.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Ah, go around the bulge of Africa and you're in Nigeria.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Or you can go over to Suez and all of a sudden you're in the Middle East and the Persian Gulf region.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And so there's a crude of plenty.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: There's multiple routes to choose from.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And not that any of them are super easy, but it's not like any of them are super complicated.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Even for the United States, back in the days before shale, when we had to import a lot,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: we could go from the West Coast to Southeast Asia.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We'd go south to Mexico and Latin America.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Or you'd go east to all those normal places in Africa and the Middle East.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: There were options. There were always options.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And that meant that the United States, even if you ignore the fact that it rules the oceans,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: still had options for keeping the lights on.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Chinese have never had that.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: By the time that China expanded to the point that it needed all the energy,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Southeast Asia was already largely tapped.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So they need to go around Singapore, by India, and into the Persian Gulf,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: where they have to deal with either the Iranians or the Saudis or the Kuwaitis or whoever else.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And that's really been the only play.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: It has always been the only play.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And that means they've had a hard time with security.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So we're posting with this video a graphic that was originally in my second book, Absent Superpower,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: that we've updated with more current data.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: This is the best data we have as of the point that COVID hit.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Because after that, the data is bleh.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: It'll be a couple more years before we get post-COVID data that's any good.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And it gives you an idea of just the scale, the volume, and the range that the Chinese have to deal with in order to get fuel.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: So starting west to east, you've got the Persian Gulf where they find themselves having to pick sides.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Everyone thinks that they're going to go with the Iranians because the Saudis have traditionally been more pro-American.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: But Saudis export an order of magnitude almost more crude than the Iranians.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Not to mention that if you side with the Iranians that you're going to have problems with the Kuwaitis or the Qataris or the Omanis.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: There's no clear answer here, except for to try to replace the United States as the dominant power within the Persian Gulf.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And the Chinese absolutely lack the military reach to do that.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Then, assuming they can get past all of those local problems, they have to get by India,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: which I don't know if you've been following the news, but for the last 80 years,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: the Indians and the Chinese haven't much cared for one another.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And while the Indian Navy is not great, the Indian Navy operates by India.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And so there's nothing, nothing that the Chinese could do if it came into a fight to protect their civilian shipping there.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Then they have to get by Singapore, which is a tight American ally,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: and each even maintains a berth for American supercarriers.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: They go within range of the missile systems that the Australians have.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: They go by the coast of Vietnam, who hates, hates, hates, hates them so much.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: They go by the Philippines, which is another U.S. ally.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And if you want to get into northern China, you now have to go by Taiwan.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And again, if you haven't been following the news, Taiwan and China don't get along very well.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And this whole time, you have to deal with both the American Navy and the Japanese Navy,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: which may have fewer ships, but they have longer range and more lethality.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: So there's, there's no solution here on the water.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The hope with Pakistan is that eventually you can build an infrastructure corridor from Pakistan up over the mountains and into western China,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: where you can at least bypass those latter series of obstacles.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The problem here is that running a pipe up and over mountain passes is really, really hard.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That's why no one does it right now.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And now if you've got local terrorists, they're just deciding to blow everything up.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: It's just one more problem.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So if there was an easy solution here, it would have been found decades ago, but there's not.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Which means that China remains the most vulnerable power of all of the major powers throughout human history.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: They're completely dependent upon an international security arrangement that they can't protect,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_02
segments.text: they can't influence, and certainly can't replace.

segments.text: Oh, one more thing.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: Well, a lot of this news is bad.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: I mean, very bad for the Chinese.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: In fact, worse than it is for any of the other major powers.

segments.text: It's not all negative.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: China's problem was with liquid fuels that are derived from oil.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So jet fuel, gasoline, diesel, things like that.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Those are the things that they're going to lose access to at scale.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: But solid fuels, most notably coal, soft, brown, low-quality coal,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: is something they have in huge volumes at home.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So even in the worst-case scenario for external security situations and energy crises,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: they're still going to be able to produce coal for their own domestic system.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So if you're willing to put up with just ridiculous carbon emissions

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: and atrocious air quality,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: the Chinese do have the ability to keep the lights on.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: They can generate electricity for all of their needs.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That's not going to save them from all of the other problems.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: But at least they won't be suffering in the cold and in the dark.
